title: Elijah, Elisha and the prophets of the north

intro.text: Five prophets of the northern kingdom of Israel: Elijah the Tishbite and Elisha son of Shaphat; Micaiah son of Imlah and Zedekiah son of Chenaanah, who stood on opposite sides before Ahab and Jehoshaphat at the gate of Samaria; and Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-hepher.
Kings sets them between the reign of Ahab and the reign of Jeroboam son of Joash.
On the reconstruction of Thiele as revised by McFall and Young, those reigns run from about 874 BC, when Ahab began, to about 753 BC, when Jeroboam II died.

Elijah and Elisha left no book: their words and deeds are told in Kings, with one writing of Elijah's in Chronicles. A book bears Jonah's name, but it is a story about him with one sentence of his preaching.

On these pages a word is said to have been fulfilled only where the text says so, as in “according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah”. Other outcomes are told as the narrative tells them, without a verdict of ours.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah is described in the text's own words: Micaiah said that the LORD had “put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets”.

prophets.name: Elijah
prophets.title: Prophet in Israel in the days of Ahab and Ahaziah
prophets.tagline: The Tishbite who shut the heaven, called fire on Carmel and went up by a whirlwind.

claim.text: Elijah told Ahab there would be no dew nor rain; in the third year he met him again and called the contest on Mount Carmel; after Naboth's death he met him in the vineyard with the LORD's sentence. When Ahab humbled himself, the word came to Elijah that the evil would come “in his son's days”.

quote.text: I have found thee: because thou hast sold thyself to work evil in the sight of the LORD.

claim.text: When Ahaziah sent to ask Baal-zebub the god of Ekron whether he would recover, Elijah turned his messengers back, then went down with the third captain and told the king himself that he would die. “So he died according to the word of the LORD which Elijah had spoken.”

quote.text: therefore thou shalt not come down off that bed on which thou art gone up, but shalt surely die.

claim.text: Chronicles alone tells that “a writing” came to Jehoram king of Judah from Elijah the prophet, naming his sins and foretelling a plague on his people and house and a disease of his bowels. Kings does not mention it.

quote.text: And there came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet

claim.text: At Horeb Elijah was told to anoint Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel. Kings records the anointing by a young prophet whom Elisha sent. As king, Jehu cited Elijah's word over Jezebel's body and again at Jezreel over the heads of Ahab's sons; Kings says he destroyed all that remained to Ahab in Samaria “according to the saying of the LORD, which he spake to Elijah”.

quote.text: for the LORD hath done that which he spake by his servant Elijah.

claim.text: At Horeb Elijah was told to “anoint Hazael to be king over Syria”. Scripture records no meeting between them; it was Elisha who told Hazael he would be king.

quote.text: As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.

claim.text: Kings records no call for Elijah. He enters the story already speaking to Ahab, named only as “the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead”; the first “word of the LORD came unto him” in the next verse.

how.text: Again and again “the word of the LORD came” to him with his next step: to hide by the brook Cherith, to go to Zarephath, to show himself to Ahab in the third year, to meet Ahab in Naboth's vineyard, and that the evil was put off to Ahab's son's days.
An angel woke him twice under the juniper tree with food for the journey; later “the angel of the LORD” sent him to meet Ahaziah's messengers and told him to go down with the third captain.

At Horeb the LORD passed by in a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, “but the LORD was not in” them; after the fire came “a still small voice”, and a voice asked him, “What doest thou here, Elijah?”
He prayed and the text records the answers: the widow's son revived, and the fire of the LORD fell on Carmel. James says he prayed that it might not rain, and prayed again for rain.
“The hand of the LORD was on Elijah” when he girded up his loins and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
Every word of his in Kings is spoken. The one written word is in Chronicles: “a writing” to Jehoram of Judah.

message.theme: The LORD, not Baal, is God

claim.text: On Carmel he put the choice to the people and prayed “that this people may know that thou art the LORD God”. When the fire fell they cried, “The LORD, he is the God”.

quotes.text: How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.
The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God.

message.theme: Rain and drought at the LORD's word

claim.text: He announced a drought without dew or rain “but according to my word”; in the third year the LORD said “I will send rain upon the earth”, and after Carmel Elijah told Ahab, “there is a sound of abundance of rain”.

quotes.text: there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.

message.theme: Is there not a God in Israel?

claim.text: Three times the same question goes to Ahaziah: does he send to Baal-zebub of Ekron because there is no God in Israel to enquire of?

quotes.text: Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron?

message.theme: Naboth's blood and the house of Ahab

claim.text: For Naboth, killed and his vineyard taken, he announced that dogs would lick Ahab's blood, that his house would be cut off like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, and that dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.

quotes.text: Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?
In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.

claim.text: At Horeb he said twice, “I, even I only, am left”; the LORD answered that he had left seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal. Paul cites the exchange in Romans 11.

quotes.text: Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him.

message.theme: Judah judged by the ways of its fathers

claim.text: The writing to Jehoram of Judah charges him with leaving the ways of Jehoshaphat and Asa, walking in the way of the kings of Israel and the house of Ahab, and killing his brothers.

quotes.text: And thou shalt have great sickness by disease of thy bowels, until thy bowels fall out by reason of the sickness day by day.

quote.text: The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth.

claim.text: He asked her for water and a morsel of bread, told her to make him a little cake first, and gave her this word from the LORD.

quote.text: go, tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah is here.

claim.text: Obadiah feared Ahab would kill him if Elijah vanished; Elijah swore he would show himself to Ahab that day.

quote.text: I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father’s house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the LORD, and thou hast followed Baalim.

claim.text: His answer when Ahab greeted him, “Art thou he that troubleth Israel?”

quote.text: How long halt ye between two opinions?

claim.text: “And the people answered him not a word.”

quote.text: Cry aloud: for he is a god; either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth, and must be awaked.

claim.text: At noon, after they had called on Baal from morning, “Elijah mocked them”.

quote.text: Get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain.
Thou hast asked a hard thing: nevertheless, if thou see me when I am taken from thee, it shall be so unto thee; but if not, it shall not be so.

claim.text: His answer when Elisha asked for “a double portion of thy spirit”. At the first meeting he had said, “Go back again: for what have I done to thee?”

quote.text: Behold, I will bring evil upon thee, and will take away thy posterity

claim.text: Spoken when Ahab met him with “Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?”

quote.text: The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.

claim.text: Part of the same word to Ahab: “And of Jezebel also spake the LORD”.

quote.text: Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron?

claim.text: The messengers went back and described him to the king: “an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins”. The king said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”

quote.text: If I be a man of God, then let fire come down from heaven, and consume thee and thy fifty.

claim.text: He said it to the first captain and, almost word for word, to the second.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast sent messengers to enquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron, is it not because there is no God in Israel to enquire of his word?
Behold, with a great plague will the LORD smite thy people, and thy children, and thy wives, and all thy goods

claim.text: Chronicles then tells that the LORD stirred up the Philistines and Arabians against Jehoram, and that “after all this the LORD smote him in his bowels with an incurable disease”.

He told Ahab there would be no dew nor rain “but according to my word”. In the third year he was sent back to Ahab with a promise of rain, and after Carmel “there was a great rain”. Luke and James give the length of the drought as “three years and six months”.
By the brook Cherith “the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening”, until the brook dried up.
At Zarephath the widow's barrel of meal did not waste and her cruse of oil did not fail, and “she, and he, and her house, did eat many days”.

When her son died, Elijah carried him to the loft, stretched himself on him three times and cried to the LORD; “the soul of the child came into him again”. She said, “Now by this I know that thou art a man of God”.

He repaired the broken altar of the LORD, building it of twelve stones, had the offering drenched three times, and prayed at the time of the evening sacrifice; “the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench”.

signs.label: The prophets of Baal at the Kishon

claim.text: “Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and slew them there.”

signs.label: A cloud like a man's hand

claim.text: On the top of Carmel he put his face between his knees and sent his servant seven times to look toward the sea; at the seventh a little cloud arose “like a man's hand”, and a great rain followed. He then ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
Fed twice by an angel, he “went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God”.

signs.label: Wind, earthquake, fire and a still small voice

claim.text: At Horeb “the LORD passed by”; the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, and after the fire came “a still small voice”. Elijah wrapped his face in his mantle.
He found Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, “passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him”.
Fire came down from heaven and consumed two captains of fifty with their men; the third captain knelt and pleaded, and the angel of the LORD told Elijah to go down with him.
He wrapped his mantle together and struck the waters, and “they were divided hither and thither, so that they two went over on dry ground”.
“There appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.”

word.text: “The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail”.

reported.text: “And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah.”

word.text: To Ahaziah: “thou shalt not come down off that bed on which thou art gone up”.

reported.text: “So he died according to the word of the LORD which Elijah had spoken.”

word.text: “The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.”

reported.text: When only her skull, feet and the palms of her hands were found, Jehu said, “This is the word of the LORD, which he spake by his servant Elijah the Tishbite”.

word.text: Against Ahab's house: “will cut off from Ahab him that pisseth against the wall”.

reported.text: Jehu said, “the LORD hath done that which he spake by his servant Elijah”; in Samaria he killed all that remained to Ahab, “according to the saying of the LORD, which he spake to Elijah”.

word.text: “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood”.

reported.text: After Ahab's death, at the pool of Samaria “the dogs licked up his blood ... according unto the word of the LORD which he spake”. Kings does not say whose word; see the open question.

claim.text: Called from the plough by the mantle, he “went after Elijah, and ministered unto him”, would not leave him on the last journey, and saw him taken. He was known as the one “which poured water on the hands of Elijah”.
He “feared the LORD greatly” and had hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel; he met Elijah during the drought and, after pleading his fear, carried his message to Ahab.
A servant went up seven times on Carmel to look toward the sea; Elijah left his servant at Beer-sheba when he fled. Neither is named.
A widow of Zarephath in the land of Zidon who fed him through the drought and whose son he raised. Jesus spoke of her in Nazareth.
Companies at Beth-el and Jericho knew he would be taken that day; fifty of them watched from afar at the Jordan. Afterwards, at their urging, Elisha let fifty strong men search three days for him.
She “cut off the prophets of the LORD”, fed the prophets of Baal and of the groves, swore to take Elijah's life after Carmel, and wrote the letters that had Naboth stoned.
Four hundred and fifty, who called on Baal from morning until the evening sacrifice, “but there was no voice, nor any that answered”.
The Jezreelite who would not sell his inheritance; after he was stoned the word of the LORD sent Elijah to meet Ahab in his vineyard.

scripture.text: As he and Elisha “still went on, and talked”, a chariot of fire and horses of fire parted them, “and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven”. Elisha cried, “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof”, and saw him no more.
Fifty strong men of the sons of the prophets searched for three days “but found him not”.
Kings records no death and no grave for Elijah.
Malachi closes: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children”.
The angel told Zacharias that his son John would “go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children”.
Asked “Art thou Elias?”, John answered, “I am not.”

Jesus said of John, “if ye will receive it, this is Elias, which was for to come”; after the transfiguration, asked why the scribes say that Elias must first come, he answered, “Elias truly shall first come, and restore all things. But I say unto you, That Elias is come already, and they knew him not”, and “the disciples understood that he spake unto them of John the Baptist”. Mark has “Elias verily cometh first” and “Elias is indeed come”.
On the mountain “there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him”; Luke adds that they “spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem”.
Some said Jesus was Elias; at the cross some heard him cry and said, “This man calleth for Elias”.
When a Samaritan village would not receive Jesus, James and John asked whether they should command fire from heaven, in the KJV's words “even as Elias did”; he rebuked them.

tradition.text: Ecclesiasticus, in the Apocrypha, praises Elias who “was taken up in a whirlwind of fire” and was “ordained for reproofs in their times ... to turn the heart of the father unto the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob”.
tradition.who: Jesus son of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus 48 (KJV Apocrypha)
tradition.when: about 200 BC on T. W. Davies's dating; scholars differ

tradition.text: Josephus writes that at this time “Elijah disappeared from among men, and no one knows of his death to this very day”, and puts him beside Enoch.

In Justin's Dialogue the Jewish speaker Trypho says, “we all expect ... that Elijah when he comes will anoint him”; Justin answers that Elijah will come before Christ's second coming, and that the Spirit of God who was in Elijah came as herald in John.
Tertullian holds that Enoch and Elijah did not die but are “reserved for the suffering of death”, to die at the time of Antichrist.
tradition.who: Tertullian, A Treatise on the Soul 50

tradition.text: Hippolytus names “the two prophets Enoch and Elias” as the two witnesses who will preach 1,260 days clothed in sackcloth before the end.
tradition.who: Hippolytus, Treatise on Christ and Antichrist 43

tradition.text: Augustine calls it “a familiar theme in the conversation and heart of the faithful” that before the judgement the Jews will believe through Elias, who will come; “we have good reason to believe that he is now alive”.

questions.question: What does “the Tishbite” mean, and where was Elijah from? The KJV says he “was of the inhabitants of Gilead” (1 Kings 17:1).

views.label: Born at a Tishbe in Galilee, living in Gilead

argument.text: Keil takes Tishbe as the town in Upper Galilee named in Tobit 1:2, Elijah's birthplace, and reads “of the settlers of Gilead” as meaning that he lived in Gilead away from his home tribe.

views.label: Josephus's retelling: “of Thesbon, a country in Gilead”
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 8.13.2 (about AD 93)

argument.text: Josephus calls Elijah “a prophet of God Almighty, of Thesbon, a country in Gilead”.

views.label: Tishbe was a place in Gilead
views.holders: “Most modern commentators”, following the Greek Septuagint (F. K. Farr, ISBE 1915, p. 930); H. Ewald and O. Thenius (as reported, and rejected, by Keil, p. 235)

argument.text: Farr writes that if the Septuagint reading is followed, as most modern commentators do, the Hebrew word read “inhabitants” or “sojourners” is itself “Tishbeh”, so that Tishbe lay in Gilead. Keil reports Thenius and Ewald for a Tishbe in Gilead and rejects it.

questions.question: 1 Kings 18:1 sends Elijah back to Ahab “in the third year”, but Luke 4:25 and James 5:17 give the drought as “three years and six months”. How do they fit?

views.label: The third year of his stay at Zarephath

argument.text: Keil counts “the third year” from Elijah's arrival at Zarephath, not from the start of the drought. He calls this the oldest view, shown by Luke and James, who give three years and six months; that length is reached only by allowing more than two years at Zarephath.

views.label: The third year of the drought
views.holders: “The Rabbins”, J. Le Clerc, O. Thenius and others (as reported by Keil)

argument.text: Keil reports that these count the third year from the beginning of the drought, the view he sets aside.

questions.question: At Horeb Elijah was told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha (1 Kings 19:15–16). Did he?

views.label: What the text records
views.holders: Our reading of the text

argument.text: Kings records that Elijah cast his mantle on Elisha; that Elisha, years later, told Hazael he would be king; and that a young prophet sent by Elisha poured oil on Jehu's head. It records no anointing by Elijah himself.

views.label: “Anoint” is used figuratively of Hazael and Elisha

argument.text: Keil holds that only Jehu was really anointed; Hazael “was merely told by Elisha that he would be king”, and Elisha was called by the cloak; the word means divine consecration to the office.

views.label: Anointed in secret by Elijah, again in public by Elisha
views.holders: Earlier interpreters (as reported, and rejected, by Keil, p. 260)

argument.text: Keil reports the opinion that Elijah anointed Hazael and Jehu at once but kept it secret, and finds it ruled out by the account of Jehu's anointing in 2 Kings 9.

questions.question: Whose word does 1 Kings 22:38 mean by “the word of the LORD which he spake”, and how does “the pool of Samaria” fit Elijah's “in the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth”?

views.label: Elijah's word, fulfilled on Ahab in part and on Joram in full

argument.text: Keil reads 22:38 as the fulfilment of Elijah's word (21:19), together with the unnamed prophet's (20:42) and Micaiah's (22:17). Because Ahab humbled himself, the threat was fulfilled on him only so far as dogs licked his blood at Samaria; it was fulfilled literally on his son Joram, whose body Jehu threw into Naboth's plot, citing the LORD's word.

views.label: Josephus's retelling: the fountain of Jezreel
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 8.15.6 (about AD 93)

argument.text: Josephus has the chariot washed “in the fountain of Jezreel”, says they then acknowledged “that the prophecy of Elijah was true”, and adds that Ahab still died at Ramoth, as Micaiah had said. Kings has “the pool of Samaria”.

questions.question: How could Elijah's writing reach Jehoram of Judah (2 Chronicles 21:12), when Kings tells Elijah's going up (2 Kings 2) before the account of Jehoram's reign (2 Kings 8:16)?

views.label: Elijah was still alive
views.holders: C. F. Keil (tr. 1872), pp. 396–398; Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: The year of Elijah's going up is nowhere stated in Scripture, so “Elijah may therefore have still been alive under Joram of Judah” (Keil). Keil reads 2 Kings 3:11 as saying only that Elisha had been Elijah's servant, not that Elijah was gone.

views.label: Written beforehand and delivered later
views.holders: Kimchi (as reported by John Gill, 1748–63); Matthew Poole (1683–85)

argument.text: Elijah foresaw Jehoram's sins and left the writing, perhaps with Elisha, to be delivered in due time.

views.label: A copyist wrote Elijah for Elisha
views.holders: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); Joseph Benson (1811–18); W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: The name was originally Elisha, who was active in Jehoshaphat's day.

views.label: Sent from heaven
views.holders: G. Menken (as reported, and rejected, by Keil, 1872, p. 398)

argument.text: Keil quotes Menken's view that if Elijah spoke again after he had been taken, “he must do it from the clouds”, and answers that Scripture knows nothing of written messages from the saints in heaven.

views.label: A later writer's composition
views.holders: E. Bertheau (as reported, and rejected, by Keil, 1872); W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: The letter in its present form comes from a later historian, or adapts Elijah's words to Jehoram's case.

questions.question: Was Malachi's “Elijah the prophet” fulfilled in John the Baptist, or is Elijah himself still to come? (Scripture's own words are under “How the story ends”.)

views.label: John came in Elijah's spirit; Elijah himself will come before the end
views.holders: Justin Martyr (Dialogue 49); Tertullian (On the Soul 35); Augustine (City of God 20.29)

argument.text: Justin says Elijah will precede the second coming and that the Spirit that was in Elijah came before the first in John. Tertullian, answering those who used Matthew 17:12 for rebirth, says John came “in the spirit and power of Elias”, not in his soul and body, and that “Elias is to come again” after his translation. Augustine expects Elias before the judgement.

views.label: Malachi's Elijah was John
views.holders: John Calvin (Harmony of the Evangelists, tr. 1845)

argument.text: Calvin reads Malachi's promise as “a simple comparison”: one like Elijah would go before the Messiah. He writes that the scribes wrongly expected Elijah the Tishbite himself to return, and paraphrases Christ's answer: the promise that Elijah would come “was true, and has been already fulfilled”.

notSaid: Kings does not name Elijah's father or tribe, and records no call.
Scripture does not say how old Elijah was, or in which year he was taken up; Kings records no death and no grave.
Kings does not say that Elijah anointed Hazael or Jehu; the anointing of Jehu is done by a young prophet Elisha sent.
Scripture does not say whether Elijah wrote anything besides the writing to Jehoram in 2 Chronicles 21:12.
The text does not say where Tishbe was; the site's map has no place for it.

prophets.name: Elisha
prophets.title: Prophet in Israel after Elijah, from the days of Joram to the days of Joash
prophets.tagline: Called from the plough by Elijah's mantle; “the man of God” of Shunem, Naaman and the siege of Samaria.

claim.text: When Joram, Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom ran out of water on the march against Moab, Elisha told Joram to go to the prophets of his father and mother, and spoke only for Jehoshaphat's sake; he promised water and victory over Moab.

quote.text: What have I to do with thee? get thee to the prophets of thy father, and to the prophets of thy mother.

person.name: “The king of Israel” of 2 Kings 5–8 (not named)

claim.text: In the stories of Naaman's letter, the Syrian raids, the blinded Syrian band, the siege of Samaria and the Shunammite's land, Kings says only “the king of Israel” or “the king”. In them the king tears his clothes at Naaman's letter, calls Elisha “My father”, swears to have his head during the famine, and asks Gehazi about Elisha's great deeds. Scripture does not say whether one king is meant throughout; the chapters stand between Joram's accession (3:1) and his death (9:24).

quote.text: See ye how this son of a murderer hath sent to take away mine head?

claim.text: It was Jehoshaphat who asked for “a prophet of the LORD” in the dry wilderness of Edom and said of Elisha, “The word of the LORD is with him”.

quote.text: were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would not look toward thee, nor see thee.

claim.text: During Ben-hadad's siege of Samaria Elisha foretold food in the gate by the next day, and it came “according to the word of the LORD”. Later, sick in Damascus, Ben-hadad sent Hazael with forty camels' burden of gifts to ask Elisha whether he would recover.

quote.text: Go, say unto him, Thou mayest certainly recover: howbeit the LORD hath shewed me that he shall surely die.

claim.text: Elisha “settled his countenance stedfastly” on Hazael and wept, and told him the evil he would do to Israel and that the LORD had shown him he would be king over Syria.

quote.text: Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel

claim.text: Elisha sent one of the children of the prophets to Ramoth-gilead with a box of oil to anoint Jehu, and to open the door and flee.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, I have anointed thee king over Israel.

claim.text: Joash came to Elisha in his last sickness and wept over him; Elisha had him shoot an arrow eastward and strike the ground, and was angry that he struck only three times. Kings then records, “Three times did Joash beat him”.

quote.text: The arrow of the LORD’s deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria

call.label: The mantle at the plough (1 Kings 19:16–21)

quote.text: Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.

claim.text: Elijah found him plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and cast his mantle on him. Elisha asked to kiss his father and mother, then slew a yoke of oxen, boiled their flesh with the oxen's gear, fed the people, “and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him”.

quote.text: I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.

claim.text: He saw Elijah taken up, took up the mantle that fell from him, struck the Jordan asking “Where is the LORD God of Elijah?”, and the waters parted. The sons of the prophets at Jericho said, “The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha.”

how.text: Many of his words carry “Thus saith the LORD”: over the spring at Jericho, to the three kings, over the twenty loaves, and to the starving city of Samaria.
Before he answered the three kings he asked for a minstrel, “and it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the LORD came upon him”.
He knew what happened out of sight: Gehazi's errand (“Went not mine heart with thee”), the Syrian king's words “in thy bedchamber”, and the king's messenger coming to take his head.
He also said when something had been hidden from him: of the Shunammite's grief, “the LORD hath hid it from me, and hath not told me”.
He spoke of what “the LORD hath shewed me” about Ben-hadad and Hazael, and prayed that his servant's eyes be opened to see the horses and chariots of fire.
He used things at hand: salt in a new cruse, meal in the pot, a stick cast in the water, and arrows shot from a window. His staff, laid on the dead child's face by Gehazi, did not wake him.

claim.text: When the king of Israel tore his clothes at Naaman's letter, Elisha sent for Naaman so that he would know there was a prophet in Israel; Naaman came back saying there was no God in all the earth but in Israel.

quotes.text: let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel.
Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel

message.theme: Deliverance from Moab and from Syria

claim.text: He promised the three kings water and victory over Moab, promised the besieged city food by the next day, and gave Joash “the arrow of deliverance from Syria”.

quotes.text: this is but a light thing in the sight of the LORD: he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand.

claim.text: He refused Naaman's gift with an oath, and when Gehazi took silver and garments from Naaman he asked, “Is it a time to receive money”.

quotes.text: As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none.

claim.text: When the blinded Syrian band was led into Samaria, he told the king not to smite them but to feed them and send them home; “So the bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel.”

quotes.text: set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master.

claim.text: He told the Shunammite that the LORD “hath called for a famine” of seven years, wept over the evil Hazael would do to Israel, and sent the oil to anoint Jehu king.

quotes.text: the LORD hath called for a famine; and it shall also come upon the land seven years.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land.
Thus saith the LORD, Make this valley full of ditches.

claim.text: Spoken in the wilderness of Edom, after the minstrel played.

words.to: A widow of the sons of the prophets

quote.text: Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest.

claim.text: Her creditor was coming to take her two sons as bondmen.

person.name: The Shunammite woman
person.note: the site's record for the people of Shunem

quote.text: About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son.

claim.text: She answered, “Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid.” Years later he told her to leave the land before a seven years' famine.

quote.text: Go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean.

claim.text: Sent by a messenger. When Naaman later asked pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon with his master, Elisha said, “Go in peace.”

quote.text: The leprosy therefore of Naaman shall cleave unto thee, and unto thy seed for ever.
Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.
Thou shalt not smite them: wouldest thou smite those whom thou hast taken captive with thy sword and with thy bow?
To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.

words.to: The lord on whose hand the king leaned

quote.text: Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.

claim.text: His answer to the lord who said, “if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?”

quote.text: The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.

claim.text: Hazael had asked, “is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?”

quote.text: Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice.

claim.text: With Elijah's mantle he struck the waters, “they parted hither and thither: and Elisha went over”.
The men of the city said the water was bad and the ground barren; he cast salt from a new cruse into the spring.

On the way up to Beth-el “little children out of the city” mocked him, “Go up, thou bald head”; he “cursed them in the name of the LORD. And there came forth two she bears out of the wood, and tare forty and two children of them.”

He told the kings, “Make this valley full of ditches”; next morning “there came water by the way of Edom, and the country was filled with water”. The Moabites saw it red as blood, came to spoil, and were beaten.
A widow of the sons of the prophets poured her one pot of oil into borrowed vessels until there was not a vessel more, “And the oil stayed.”
The woman of Shunem who had made him a chamber on the wall had no child and an old husband; she “bare a son at that season that Elisha had said unto her”.

The boy died on his mother's knees; she rode to Elisha at Carmel. The staff Gehazi laid on him did nothing; Elisha shut the door, prayed, and lay upon the child, and “the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes”.
At Gilgal in a dearth, wild gourds made the pottage deadly; he cast meal into the pot, “And there was no harm in the pot.”

signs.label: Twenty loaves for a hundred men

claim.text: A man from Baal-shalisha brought twenty barley loaves; his servitor asked, “should I set this before an hundred men?”, and “they did eat, and left thereof”.
Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria and a leper, dipped himself seven times in Jordan, “and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean”.
“He went out from his presence a leper as white as snow.”
A borrowed axe head fell into the Jordan; Elisha cut a stick and cast it in, “and the iron did swim”.

signs.label: Horses and chariots of fire at Dothan

claim.text: When a Syrian host surrounded Dothan, he prayed and his servant saw “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha”. The Syrians were struck with blindness “according to the word of Elisha”, led into Samaria, fed and sent home.
“The Lord had made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots”; they fled, four lepers found the camp empty, and flour and barley sold in the gate of Samaria at the price he had named.
He told the Shunammite to leave before a seven years' famine; she sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years, and her land was restored while Gehazi was telling the king about her son.
On his deathbed he put his hands on the king's hands on the bow and had him shoot eastward, then told him to strike the ground; the king struck three times.

After his death, in a year when bands of Moabites invaded, men burying a man “spied a band of men” and cast the body into Elisha's sepulchre; “when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet”.

reported.text: “So the waters were healed unto this day, according to the saying of Elisha which he spake.”

word.text: “About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son.”

reported.text: She “bare a son at that season that Elisha had said unto her, according to the time of life”.

word.text: “They shall eat, and shall leave thereof.”

reported.text: “They did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the LORD.”

word.text: “Go and wash in Jordan seven times”.

reported.text: Naaman “dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God” and was clean.

word.text: His prayer: “Smite this people, I pray thee, with blindness.”

reported.text: “And he smote them with blindness according to the word of Elisha.”

word.text: “To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel”.

reported.text: “So a measure of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD.”

word.text: To the doubting lord: “thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof”.

reported.text: The people trod on him in the gate “and he died, as the man of God had said”; “And so it fell out unto him”.

claim.text: His master, who called him with the mantle; Elisha would not leave him on the road to the Jordan and cried after him, “My father, my father”.
Elisha is “the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah”; at his call he asked to kiss his father and mother first.

His servant, who called the Shunammite, ran with the staff, took silver and garments from Naaman in his master's name and was struck with leprosy; later he told the king “all the great things that Elisha hath done”.

person.note: the site's record for the people of Shunem

claim.text: “A great woman” of Shunem who fed him and made him a chamber; her son was born and raised again at his word, and her land was restored after the famine.
At Gilgal in the dearth they sat before him and he had pottage made for them; he went with them to the Jordan to build a larger dwelling, and sent one of them to anoint Jehu.
The Syrian captain whom he cleansed; Naaman asked for two mules' burden of earth, vowing to offer only to the LORD.
“The young man the prophet” whom Elisha sent; he anointed Jehu in an inner chamber, gave him the charge against the house of Ahab and fled. The captains called him “this mad fellow”.

person.name: The lord on whose hand the king leaned

claim.text: He doubted the promise of food: “if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?”; he was set over the gate and trodden down there.

scripture.text: “Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died.” Joash king of Israel came down and wept over him, “O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof”, the words Elisha had cried when Elijah was taken.
“And Elisha died, and they buried him.”
When a dead man was cast into his sepulchre and touched his bones, “he revived, and stood up on his feet”.
Jesus said in Nazareth, “many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian.”
Kings does not say where he was buried or how old he was.

tradition.text: Ecclesiasticus says “Eliseus was filled with his spirit”, that “he was not moved with the presence of any prince”, and that “after his death his body prophesied”.
tradition.who: Jesus son of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus 48 (KJV Apocrypha)
tradition.when: about 200 BC on T. W. Davies's dating; scholars differ

tradition.text: Josephus adds that Elisha “obtained a magnificent funeral”, and says that “certain robbers” cast a man they had slain into his grave.
Jerome writes that at Samaria, renamed Sebaste, “There lie the prophets Elisha and Obadiah and John the Baptist”.
tradition.when: written after Paula's death in AD 404

questions.question: What did Elisha ask for in “a double portion of thy spirit” (2 Kings 2:9)?

views.label: The firstborn's share
views.holders: C. F. Keil (tr. 1872), pp. 292–293, following Levi ben Gershom, Grotius and Hengstenberg

argument.text: Keil bases the request on Deuteronomy 21:17, where the firstborn receives a double portion of his father's inheritance: Elisha asked, as Elijah's firstborn among the sons of the prophets, for the heir's share of his spirit.

views.label: Twice Elijah's measure
views.holders: Translators from Ephraem Syrus to Köster and F. W. Krummacher, Luther following the Vulgate; J. Le Clerc and A. Pfeiffer on Elisha's miracles (as reported, and rejected, by Keil, pp. 292–293)

argument.text: Keil reports that many took it as a double measure of Elijah's spirit, some pointing to Elisha's many and greater miracles, and answers that the words do not mean this.

questions.question: How is the curse on the children of Bethel (2 Kings 2:23–24) to be read?

views.label: A judgement for mocking the LORD's prophet

argument.text: Keil takes them as boys from Bethel, “the chief seat of the idolatrous calf-worship”, who knew Elisha and in his person insulted the prophet of the LORD; the LORD, not Elisha, carried out the curse.

views.label: A plan of the city's rulers
views.holders: O. von Gerlach (as reported by Keil, p. 300)

argument.text: Keil reports Gerlach's suggestion that the rulers of the city had planned the mockery out of enmity to the prophet and put the children forward, and says there is no need for it.

views.label: Not historical
views.holders: O. Thenius (as reported by Keil, p. 300)

argument.text: Keil reports that Thenius adduced the supposed “immorality of cursing” as a disproof of the historical truth of the story.

questions.question: Did Elisha tell Hazael to say “Thou mayest certainly recover” (the KJV), or “Thou wilt not live” (2 Kings 8:10)?

views.label: “Thou wilt live”, as the KJV
views.holders: Most commentators, the ancient versions and the Masoretes (as reported by Keil, p. 334)

argument.text: Keil reports that most follow the Hebrew margin's reading, so that Elisha tells Hazael to say the king will recover, though the LORD has shown he will die.

views.label: “Thou wilt not live”, the written Hebrew

argument.text: Keil prefers the written text, so that Elisha's answer was that the king would not live, and Hazael's report of recovery (verse 14) was his own.

views.label: What the text gives
views.holders: Our count from the text

argument.text: Kings first shows him at work after Elijah's going up, which it tells after Ahaziah's death, and last at Joash's visit to his deathbed. Between them Kings gives Joram twelve years, Jehu twenty-eight and Jehoahaz seventeen; it does not say in which years his work began or ended.

views.label: About fifty years after Elijah's going up

argument.text: Keil, discussing the word “bald head”, says Elisha “lived for fifty years after this”, citing 2 Kings 13:14.

notSaid: Scripture does not name the king of Israel in 2 Kings 5–8, the king of Syria in Naaman's story, or the Shunammite woman.
Kings does not give Elisha's age, or say where he was buried.
Scripture does not explain how Gehazi, after his leprosy, was talking with the king in 2 Kings 8:4–5.
Kings does not say whether Elisha ever met Jehu; the anointing was done by the young prophet he sent.
Elisha wrote no book, and Scripture records no writing of his.

prophets.name: Micaiah
otherNames: Micaiah the son of Imla (2 Chronicles 18)
prophets.title: Prophet of the LORD in the days of Ahab, the one Ahab said he hated
prophets.tagline: One man against four hundred: “what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.”

claim.text: Ahab named him as one more prophet “by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil”. Micaiah foretold Israel scattered and the LORD's evil word against him; Ahab sent him to prison “until I come in peace”. Chronicles tells the scene almost word for word.

quote.text: If thou return at all in peace, the LORD hath not spoken by me.

claim.text: Micaiah was sent for because Jehoshaphat, after hearing the four hundred, asked for “a prophet of the LORD besides”, and answered Ahab's complaint with “Let not the king say so”.

quote.text: Is there not here a prophet of the LORD besides, that we might enquire of him?

how.text: He bound himself by oath, before he reached the king: “what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.”
His first answer repeated the four hundred: “Go, and prosper”. Only when the king adjured him to tell “nothing but that which is true” did he tell what he had seen.
He spoke in visions: “I saw all Israel scattered upon the hills”, and “I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him”.

Kings and Chronicles side by side. Ahab's complaint: “he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil” (Kings), “he never prophesied good unto me, but always evil” (Chronicles). Micaiah's oath: “what the LORD saith unto me” (Kings), “even what my God saith” (Chronicles). His first answer in Chronicles: “Go ye up, and prosper, and they shall be delivered into your hand”. The spirit offers to “persuade” Ahab in Kings and to “entice” him in Chronicles; Kings has “all these thy prophets”, Chronicles “these thy prophets”. His last word is “If thou return at all in peace” in Kings; Chronicles words the condition with a different adverb. Chronicles has no dogs at the pool of Samaria.

claim.text: The messenger asked him to speak like the others; he swore to speak only what the LORD said.

quotes.text: As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.

claim.text: He saw Israel scattered on the hills “as sheep that have not a shepherd”, and the LORD said, “These have no master”.

quotes.text: I saw all Israel scattered upon the hills, as sheep that have not a shepherd: and the LORD said, These have no master: let them return every man to his house in peace.

message.theme: A lying spirit in the prophets' mouths

claim.text: He saw the LORD ask “Who shall persuade Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?”, and a spirit offer to be “a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets”.

quotes.text: Now therefore, behold, the LORD hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets, and the LORD hath spoken evil concerning thee.

quote.text: As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.
Hear thou therefore the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.

claim.text: Spoken in the open place at the gate of Samaria, where the two kings sat on their thrones.

quote.text: Behold, thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself.

claim.text: His answer when Zedekiah struck him on the cheek.

quote.text: Hearken, O people, every one of you.

claim.text: Chronicles: “Hearken, all ye people.”
He saw all Israel scattered upon the hills “as sheep that have not a shepherd”.
He saw the host of heaven on the LORD's right hand and left, one saying one thing and another another, until a spirit came forth to persuade Ahab.
Kings and Chronicles name him only as Micaiah's father (Chronicles spells it “Imla”).
One of the four hundred; he made horns of iron and struck Micaiah on the cheek.
“About four hundred men”, who all said “Go up”; the messenger said they “declare good unto the king with one mouth”.
Micaiah was to be carried “back unto Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king's son”.
Named with Amon as the one Micaiah was taken back to.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: The gate of Samaria, where the kings sat

places.name: Ramoth-gilead
places.note: The city Ahab went up to take

scripture.text: Ahab ordered: “Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace.” Micaiah's last recorded words are his answer.

Ahab went up to Ramoth-gilead disguised; an arrow drawn “at a venture” struck him between the joints of the harness, and he “died at even”. A cry went through the host, “Every man to his city, and every man to his own country.”
Chronicles tells the same and ends “about the time of the sun going down he died”.
Scripture does not say what became of Micaiah after he was led away.

tradition.text: Josephus makes Micaiah the prophet who disguised himself and condemned Ahab for letting Ben-hadad go (1 Kings 20), and says Ahab already had him in prison for foretelling that he would be “overcome and slain by the king of Syria”.

questions.question: Is Micaiah the unnamed prophet who condemned Ahab after the war with Ben-hadad (1 Kings 20:35–43)?

views.label: Yes
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 8.14.5 (about AD 93); “the Rabbins” (as reported by Keil)

argument.text: Josephus names the disguised prophet of 1 Kings 20 Micaiah, and has Ahab put him in prison for it.

views.label: No ground for it

argument.text: Keil calls the identification “mere conjecture”, while inferring from “carry him back” (22:26) that Ahab had already imprisoned Micaiah for an unwelcome prophecy.

questions.question: How could the LORD put “a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets” (1 Kings 22:23)?

views.label: A judgement on Ahab, not mere permission

argument.text: Keil takes the spirit as “the personified spirit of prophecy”, not Satan, and holds that the LORD gave Ahab up in his unbelief to be deceived by his prophets as a judgement; Keil adds that “thou wilt also be able” leaves room for resistance.

views.label: God's permission
views.holders: “The fathers and the earlier theologians” (as reported by Keil, p. 277)

argument.text: Keil reports that these read “Persuade Ahab, thou wilt be able” and “Jehovah has put a lying spirit” as expressing only God's permission, and disagrees.

notSaid: Scripture records no call for Micaiah and no other prophecy than this one scene.
Kings and Chronicles do not say whether Micaiah was released, or how his story ended.
Scripture does not say why Ahab had to “carry him back” to Amon (1 Kings 22:26), or for what earlier word.

prophets.name: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah
prophets.title: One of Ahab's four hundred prophets, of whom Micaiah said “the LORD hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets” (1 Kings 22:23)
prophets.tagline: He made horns of iron, promised victory over Syria and struck Micaiah on the cheek.

claim.text: Before Ahab and Jehoshaphat at the gate of Samaria he made horns of iron and spoke in the LORD's name, and all the prophets prophesied so. Chronicles tells it the same way.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them.

claim.text: Jehoshaphat heard the four hundred and still asked, “Is there not here a prophet of the LORD besides, that we might enquire of him?”

how.text: He spoke with “Thus saith the LORD” and acted it out with a sign, the horns of iron.
He claimed the Spirit: “Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?”

Kings and Chronicles side by side: Kings has “With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them” and “smote Micaiah on the cheek”; Chronicles has “With these thou shalt push Syria until they be consumed” and “smote Micaiah upon the cheek”. His question about the Spirit is the same in both.

claim.text: With the horns he promised that the king would push the Syrians “until thou have consumed them”, and all the prophets said, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and prosper”.

quotes.text: Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and prosper: for the LORD shall deliver it into the king’s hand.

quote.text: With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them.
Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?

claim.text: He “went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek” as he said it.
“Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron”.
Named only as Zedekiah's father.
Ahab gathered “about four hundred men”; they all said “Go up”, and the messenger said they declared good “with one mouth”.
The prophet who said the LORD had put a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab's prophets, and whom Zedekiah struck.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: The void place at the gate of Samaria

places.name: Ramoth-gilead
places.note: Where he told the king to go up

scripture.text: Micaiah answered him: “thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself.”
The king went up to Ramoth-gilead, was struck by an arrow and died at even.
Scripture does not mention Zedekiah again, and does not say whether he hid in an inner chamber.

tradition.text: Josephus gives Zedekiah a speech: Elijah, “a better prophet”, had said the dogs would lick Ahab's blood in Jezreel, so Micaiah, who said the king would be slain three days' journey away, must be lying; then he struck Micaiah, saying, “let him then hurt my hand”.

questions.question: Who were the four hundred prophets? They spoke in the LORD's name (1 Kings 22:11–12), yet Jehoshaphat asked for “a prophet of the LORD besides” (22:7).

views.label: Prophets of the LORD under the calf worship

argument.text: Keil calls them prophets of the LORD “worshipped under the image of an ox”, who “practised prophesying as a trade without any call from God”.

views.label: True prophets of the LORD
views.holders: J. Le Clerc and O. Thenius (as reported, and rejected, by Keil, p. 274)

argument.text: Keil reports that these took them to be “true prophets of Jehovah and disciples of the prophets”.

views.label: Prophets of Baal or of the groves
views.holders: “Some of the earlier commentators” (as reported, and rejected, by Keil, p. 274)

argument.text: Keil reports that some identified them with the prophets of Baal or the four hundred prophets of the groves of 1 Kings 18:19, and answers that Ahab could not have enquired of the LORD through them.

questions.question: Did Micaiah's word to Zedekiah, about hiding in an inner chamber, come to pass?

views.label: Scripture does not say
views.holders: Our reading of the text

argument.text: Neither Kings nor Chronicles mentions Zedekiah after Micaiah's answer.

views.label: Probably, after the battle

argument.text: Keil thinks it was “probably fulfilled at the close of the war”, when Jezebel or Ahab's friends made the prophets suffer, “although there is nothing said about this in our history”.

notSaid: Scripture does not say who sent Zedekiah or whom he served besides the king, and gives no other word of his.
Neither Kings nor Chronicles says what happened to Zedekiah after the scene at the gate.
The text does not call him a “false prophet”; it reports Micaiah's word about a lying spirit in the mouth of all the king's prophets.

prophets.name: Jonah
prophets.title: Prophet of Israel in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, sent to Nineveh
prophets.tagline: He foretold Israel's restored borders, fled from a call to Nineveh, and preached there.

claim.text: Kings says Jeroboam restored Israel's coast “according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah”, because the LORD saw that Israel's affliction was very bitter.

quote.text: He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain

claim.text: When the word reached him, he rose from his throne, covered himself with sackcloth, sat in ashes, and decreed a fast for man and beast. The book does not name him.

quote.text: Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?
Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.

claim.text: “The word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai”; he “rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD”, went down to Joppa and paid the fare.

quote.text: Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee.

claim.text: “So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD.”

how.text: “The word of the LORD came unto Jonah”, once at the start of the book and again “the second time”.
Kings gives the outcome of his word to Jeroboam's Israel but not its words.
In Nineveh his preaching is given as one sentence: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”
He prayed from the fish's belly, and prayed again in anger when Nineveh was spared; the LORD answered him with questions.

tradition.text: Josephus retells the story, sends the ship to “Tarsus, in Cilicia”, says “it is also reported” that a whale vomited Jonah out “upon the Euxine Sea”, and gives his preaching as that Nineveh would “lose the dominion of Asia”.
A Jewish tradition reported by Jerome made Jonah the son of the widow of Zarephath whom Elijah raised; Keil calls it “nothing more than a Jewish Hagada”.

questions.question: How is the book of Jonah to be read? (Views in the order they are argued in these sources: the historical reading first.)

views.label: A true history
views.holders: E. B. Pusey (1860s; printing of 1869), pp. 248, 255; C. F. Keil (tr. 1868), pp. 380–388; J. R. Sampey (ISBE 1915), who names Keil, Pusey, Delitzsch, Orelli and J. Kennedy as holding it

argument.text: Pusey writes that “Our Lord relates it as a fact”. Keil argues that Jonah's three days could be a type of Christ's death and resurrection only if they had “as much objective reality as the facts of the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ”, and so the book “relates historical facts”.

views.label: A teaching story on a basis of fact

argument.text: Driver finds “indications that it is not strictly historical” and a chiefly “didactic purpose”, but holds that the materials “rest ultimately upon a basis of fact” and that Jonah's preaching at Nineveh was successful, “though not upon the scale represented in the book”.

views.label: A parable

argument.text: Smith writes that the book does not “claim to be real history” but “offers to us all the marks of the parable or allegory”: the three days in the fish, the general account of Nineveh's conversion, and the abrupt close once the moral is plain.

views.label: An allegory of Israel's exile and return
views.holders: O. Kleinert, T. K. Cheyne and C. H. H. Wright (as reported by Driver, 1891, p. 304)

argument.text: On this view, as Driver summarises it, Jonah stands for Israel, which shrank from its calling, was “swallowed up” by Babylon and brought back, and then was disappointed that judgement on the nations did not come.

questions.question: Who wrote the book of Jonah, and when?

views.label: Jonah himself, in the eighth century
views.holders: E. B. Pusey, p. 248; C. F. Keil, pp. 380–381

argument.text: Pusey: “The history of his mission, Jonah doubtless himself wrote”, citing Jewish tradition and the book's place among the prophets. Keil answers the arguments from Aramaic words and the psalm.

views.label: After the exile, perhaps the fifth century BC

argument.text: Driver argues from the style, the psalm in chapter 2, the teaching it presupposes and the unnamed king that it was written “long after the lifetime of Jonah himself”, and says a fifth-century date “will probably not be far wide of the truth”.

views.label: Possibly as late as about 300 BC

argument.text: Smith says that if the book quotes Joel, it would come down to “probably about 300 B.C.”, which, he says, still leaves time for its reception into the Prophets, closed by 200 BC on his view.

views.label: Unknown
views.holders: J. R. Sampey (ISBE 1915), p. 1729

argument.text: Sampey: the book “is anonymous, and we really do not know who the author was or when he lived”; the view that Jonah wrote it “has not been made wholly untenable”.

questions.question: What do Jesus' sayings about Jonah (Matthew 12:39–41; 16:4; Luke 11:29–32) say about how the book should be read?

views.label: He treated the events as real
views.holders: C. F. Keil, p. 388; E. B. Pusey, p. 255; J. R. Sampey (ISBE 1915), p. 1729

argument.text: Sampey: “we still think that Our Lord regarded the miracles of the fish and the repentance of the Ninevites as actual events”; Keil and Pusey argue the same.

views.label: His words fit either reading

argument.text: Smith grants that the words “are compatible with the opinion that the Book of Jonah is a record of real fact”, but holds that “Christ is using an illustration”, which may come from fact or from story.

notSaid: Kings does not record the words of Jonah's prophecy to Jeroboam's Israel, only what came of it.
The book does not name the king of Nineveh, say where the fish cast Jonah up, or say what Jonah did after the LORD's last question.
Scripture does not say when or where Jonah died.
The book does not say that Jonah wrote it; it speaks of him in the third person.
